messages.subject: RSFs
parts:
Hi Chris,

With your advice I was able to effectively estimate home ranges for pumas, thank you!

For the next stage of my analysis I need to produce RSFs for each puma for: a) all locations within home range, b) known feeding sites, c) known bed sites, and d) random unused locations. I want to do this so I can compare RSFs across the 4 categories to determine how habitat might be differentially selected according to each category.  

I am aware that the rsf.fit function in development within ctmm would allow me to use all location data, while accounting for the autocorrelation between locations and any irregular fix intervals. However, based on my very limited understanding, to allow comparison between RSFs I believe I would need to build all RSFs using the same modelling approach ...? Hence, I may need to resort to the traditional method of thinning the data to reduce autocorrelation for the "all locations within home range" category. 

Is there any way that you know of that I could achieve the comparison across all 4 categories without having to thin the "all locations within home range"? 

Any advice or suggestions are very helpful.

Many thanks, 

Luke

I'm not exactly sure what you want to do, but you can always compare relative suitability values at different points and across individuals. You just don't want to be comparing absolute suitability values across individuals, regardless of whether you are doing regular RSFs or iRSFs.

Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

I have a question about creating seasonal RSFs and I just wanted to check that I understand the correct approach.

We are wanting to assess the influence of study area/population level factors (including the presence or not of wolves, bears, and/or puma hunting by humans) on the selection of critical habitat characteristics (specifically feeding/kill sites and bed sites) of pumas. We have GPS collar data for multiple pumas across multiple study areas in both North and South America and multiple kill and bed sites for each puma. Study areas are exposed to differing combinations of external factors (i.e. wolves, bears, humans). So, we are more interested in what is happening at a population level per study area rather than at the individual puma level. I understand we can derive population level parameters from RSFs by placing individual estimates in a list and calculating mean().

Given the presence of bears and hunting are seasonal, it would seem prudent that we create seasonal RSFs. Below is a potential workflow:

Habitat selection per seasonal home range:
- Split all movement/location data for each puma according to season (e.g. winter vs summer)
- Calculate akdes per season
- Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual, using seasonal akdes and location data (I think NDVI will be the only time dependent variable being used in the RSFS, so we should use mean summer NDVI for summer RSF, and use mean winter NDVI for winter RSF)
- Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean() 

Habitat selection for bed and kill sites per season:
- Split kill and bed sites by season
- Create separate RSFs for winter and summer for each individual for kill sites and bed sites, using seasonal akdes and kill and bed site locations
- Calculate population level/study area RSF parameter estimates using mean() 

Hence, I was thinking of creating the following 9 RSFs per individual before deriving population level parameter estimates:
1. all locations
2. all kill sites
3. all bed sites
4. winter only locations
5. winter only kill sites
6. winter only bed sites
7. summer locations
8. summer kill sites
9. summer bed sites

Questions:
1. Is the above workflow appropriate to account for potential seasonal differences in habitat selection by pumas?

2. If an individual puma is monitored across multiple years and therefore multiple seasons (e.g. 3 winters and 2 summers), do I need to calculate individual akdes per season per year (i.e. 1st akde for winter 1, 2nd akde for winter 2, 3rd akde for winter 3, etc) and then calculate the mean akde before RSF fitting, to account for the large gap in time between seasons and the influence on range-residency assumption? Or can I just create a single seasonal akde from the beginning, despite a large time gap between the same season across multiple years?

3. If I want to assess seasonal habitat selection, do I need to first create a seasonal akde (i.e. Winter kill site selection should only be assessed relative to winter akde, not the entire akde across all seasons)?

Regards,
Luke.

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: RSFs
parts:
Hi Luke,
  1. Until I have time-dependent raster (time-stack/brick) support, yes this would be the approach.
  2. You can fit one movement model (and UD) to the same seasons over multiple years, as long as the puma did not migrate/disperse or radically change behavior in some other way. The gaps do not impede the calculation - they just make the variogram ugly where there is no data.
  3. That's what I would do, unless the seasonal data were very limited and space use across season was not very variable.
Best,
Chris

1.     Should I use rsf.fit() or rsf.select() to determine mean() RSF parameter estimates for the population? 

       I have produced one UD per individual puma using akde() and I want to calculate the mean RSF parameter estimates for the puma population at each study site. I have chosen 5 to 7 predictor variables that I think are potentially important drivers of habitat selection by pumas. I have tested both rsf.fit and rsf.select on the same data (using unmasked rasters) and it appears that only rsf.fit returns parameter estimates (for all variables included in the raster list, or specific variables if formula included), whereas rsf.select tests all combinations of predictor variables and assesses model performance rather than providing parameter estimates.

Given this, would the correct approach be just to run rsf.fit using all the predictor variables for each individual and derive mean() population level parameter estimates? If I were to run rsf.select first, I would likely end up with a different best model for each individual and hence I couldn’t calculate mean population parameter estimates if each best fit model does not contain the same predictor variables – this approach may also make comparison across study areas difficult. Is this correct?

parts:
Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

  1. I would only select one model. The problem with model averaging is how do you average the covariances. If the averaged models share predictors or have colinear predictors, then the conventional way of averaging covariances as if the models are independent will underestimate uncertainties.
  2. I don't have a reference for this, specifically. The existing RSF meta-analysis work that I know just assumed the same parameters for each individual, but did recognize that some could be missing and didn't propose anything for that IIRC.

  4. I need to fix the documentation, standardize was called rescale previously. This will only happen with no formula argument or a trivial formula argument.
    Standardizing the predictors is generally good for numerical stability and optimization in regression analysis.

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

  1. I would only select one model. The problem with model averaging is how do you average the covariances. If the averaged models share predictors or have colinear predictors, then the conventional way of averaging covariances as if the models are independent will underestimate uncertainties.
  2. I don't have a reference for this, specifically. The existing RSF meta-analysis work that I know just assumed the same parameters for each individual, but did recognize that some could be missing and didn't propose anything for that IIRC.
  3. The offset variable does need to be a boolean (1|0). Having to call stats::offset will be fixed in the next push.
  4. I need to fix the documentation, standardize was called rescale previously. This will only happen with no formula argument or a trivial formula argument.
    Standardizing the predictors is generally good for numerical stability and optimization in regression analysis.
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

I'll have it in the next week or two - I'm just extremely busy at this moment and prioritizing bug fixes over feature requests.

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

I'll have it in the next week or two - I'm just extremely busy at this moment and prioritizing bug fixes over feature requests.

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

  1. rsf.select() will not enforce that model structure, but you can have verbose=TRUE and then select from only candidate models that you believe have the appropriate biological structure. However, I could imagine a selection like ~tree_cover:day_time that would not necessarily have the main effect of tree_cover, and day_time would never be a main effect in a spatial point-process model (rsf.fit() should turn that off if you try it).
  2. You would want to structure the models so that you are selecting among a null model, a model with an overall main effect, and a model with an overall main effect + an interaction that is on-average zero and provides extra detail to the main-effect model. If you don't or can't structure the models so that the interpretations are the same as you add predictors, then you could very well end up averaging coefficients nonsensically.
  3. Yes, but I would recommend a simple rescaling of the predictors so that you never worry about back transforming.
  4. For the moment, you need to remove those points at the beginning of the analysis, but I'm going to try to have an argument for that in rsf.fit() within a couple of weeks. But removing those data points is not the same as making that area unavailable in the RSF model.
Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. Best,
Chris

  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

1.a) You want to include selected models to avoid ill-conditioned covariance matrices, but that selection needn't be strong. You don't need to test for significance.

mean() allows for missing predictors. You just need to structure the interactions consistently. For instance:

~ tree_cover + tree_cover:day

could equivalently be modeled as

~tree_cover + tree_cover:night

or

~tree_cover:day + tree_cover:night

but you want a consistent choice here that also makes sense for model selection to first be able to select the largest overall effect and then be able to refine that with additional terms.

1.b) Looks fine to me.
2.) With the null model, NA predictor values aren't ensured to work when the predictors aren't being used, whereas offset()will be maintained going forward.
3.) I'm not sure what you are asking here. How do you plan to make this comparison?

Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Chris,

After lengthy discussions with my project collaborators about the best approach for our analysis given the limitations of our data (e.g. small sample sizes for some individuals), we have decided to go with a more traditional approach to the RSF analysis (i.e used-available approach using logistic regression modelling) rather than rsf.fit(), whilst being aware of the drawbacks of doing so.

We have decided to take this approach for a couple of reasons: 
i) Retain flexibility in our approach: This will allow us to use just random intercept only models if we need to so we can assess all data, BUT if sample sizes allow, we can also try running random slope models to account for individual variability. We have concerns over the low numbers of kill or bed sites for some individuals and don't want our sample size of individual animals to be reduced by only modelling RSFs individually in rsf.fit().
ii) Assessing habitat selection relative to entire home range rather just a small section of the home range in the case of bed and kill site habitat selection: As you pointed out previously, for assessing kill or bed site selection we would need to generate separate UDs per set of kill or bed sites per individual animal, but given this can be as few as 5 to 10 kill or bed sites for some animals, the UD created will not cover the entire home range and will therefore not be assessing habitat selection of kill or bed sites relative to the entire home range, but instead just a small fraction of it. Additionally, we want to compare selection across the home range using all tracking data vs bed sites vs kill sites. Ultimately we we want to predict kill and bed site habitat across the landscape and determine the proportion of these areas within each individual's home range.


Given we are going with a more traditional approach, we are going to generate a certain number available points per used point (somewhere in the range of 10-100 as per Muff et al. 2019. We may also do some type of sensitivity analysis to determine threshold) my questions are:

1. Would it be suitable to use the weights generated in akde(), that are assigned to each location, in subsequent logistic regression models using all the tracking data within a traditional used-available approach? Will the weights still be accounting for autocorrelation/pseudoreplication and irregularities in fix rates and fix success, OR are they only valid with a suitable movement model? Or by using a traditional approach will there be no movement model and locations will be considered to be IID and the weights are still useful? 
Note: Weights aren't a concern for the kill and bed sites because we can consider these independent locations, however we want to generate RSFs for all the location/tracking data so we can compare how habitat selection compares between all data vs kill sites vs bed sites, relative to what is available in the individual's home range.

2. Would using these weights mean we wouldn't need to assign an arbitrary large weight to available points (e.g. 1000 or more) as described in Muff et al. 2019, or would it be wise to do both using the traditional used-available logistic regression approach?

3. Do the weights generated and assigned by akde() also account for the error (e.g. DOP) associated with each GPS location/fix? 

4. Fix success varies between 15% to 97% across individuals, with 66 of 76 animals with a fix success rate of <80%. However, it appears that assigning of weights using akde() deals with this issue and I don't need to go down the path of assessing potential habitat-biased fix success (e.g. 1/Pfix as per Frair et al. 2010), given Alston et al. 2022 states: "As an additional benefit, likelihood weights can also account for sampling biases that arise from irregular sampling. Such bias can occur, for example, when covariates are over- or under-sampled, such as when environmental covariates are associated with differential probability of successful triangulation of animal locations (Fleming et al., 2018; Frair et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2007)." Is this because the irregular, or more temporally isolated fixes, are given greater weight because they are less correlated with other fixes, and hence it accounts for sampling irregularities due to collar failure or habitat effects, etc.?

~ tree_cover + tree_cover:day

~tree_cover + tree_cover:night

~tree_cover:day + tree_cover:night

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

i. Random intercepts don't really do anything: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.13087
Random slopes are worth trying if you can't get anything out of the individual RSFs but want to try to get something out of the population. You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). But not accounting for the autocorrelation is also going to return false positives, so if you don't address that, then you might think you are getting something out but are just getting noise.

ii. I don't see the issue, but maybe I'm not fully understand what you are doing. The distribution of kill/bet sites is what it is. Either the data are representative of that distribution or the sample is biased, and if its the latter, then you would have to adjust for that in some other way in the model.

Definitely do a sensitivity analysis on the parameter estimates by doubling the number of available points until convergence.

1. It depends on how the weights enter into the model - they need to weight the log-likelihood itself. If you can give me a reference, then I can tell you. But, in principle, yes.

2. You need both, because you are using glm as a round-about way of approximating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model. The weights used in rsf.fit() don't need to include that because ctmm is directly evaluating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model.

3. Not yet, but I'm about to put in support for that.

4. Yes.

Best,
Chris

The standardization in rsf.fit() is the simplistic z-score, which is disabled when you use a formula, because something like square terms or interaction terms means that the code doesn't know how to back-transform the betas. If using those terms, it is up to you to standardize/normalize your predictors before rsf.fit() and I would suggest something simple, like if one predictor is aspect angles between 0 and 90 degrees by definition, then dividing by 90 will give values that have a mean and standard deviation not too different from 1, which is what you want. What you don't want to do is to standardize/normalize the predictors differently on different datasets if you aren't going to back-transform the corresponding betas.

Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,
  1. rsf.select() with verbose=TRUE returns the list of candidate models, and you can run summary() on any model in that list to see their parameter estimates, with the first model being the selected model.
    In general, you do not want to feed non-selected models into mean() because unsupported features can cause numerical errors in the covariance matrix, and the covariance matrix is used in the meta-analysis weights. Unsupported features also aren't really going to be contributing very much information to the population estimates, anyhow.
    mean() can handle different individuals having different selected parameters.
  2. As a simple rule I would use rsf.select() before mean(), but the second model here probably wouldn't hurt anything because its within an AIC/parameter.
  3. I can add an argument to drop NA location fixes - I'll add that to the to-do list.
    Regarding the formula error, do you have the stats package loaded? Maybe try stats::offset(). I'll look into my code - I probably have set the formula environment incorrectly.
  4. Yes, in any regression context, a categorical variable with N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables with N-1 regression parameters. Therefore, you might consider more parsimonious candidate models where some of those categories are combined in a reasonable way, and rsf.select() will not do this for you.
  5. Yes, that is the approximate correction for the autocorrelation - using the autocorrelated Gaussian effective sample size rather than the nominal sample size: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14025
  6. i. In any regression context, N categories is expanded into N-1 indicator variables that are relative to the reference category, which must be sampled. Here your predictors are 0 relative to 4, 1 relative to 4, 2 relative to 4, and 3 relative to 4. You can only ever estimate a categorical effect relative to a different category (or some combination thereof).
    ii. If you have finely sampled raster data and aren't using a non-stationary model, then it should be faster to use Riemann.
    iii. level.UD is only used for conventional non-integrated analyses, which is not recommended.
    iv. With Monte-Carlo integration, you might adjust error for computational speed when setting up an analysis, otherwise you probably wouldn't touch those in normal use.
  7. Yes and yes, but its better to use model selection to help tease out the significant parameters as unsupported parameters can potentially corrupt the covariance matrix estimate with numerical error.
  8. The model-fit summary contains Gaussian area estimates and Gaussian RMS speed estimates. The akde() and speed() estimates are non-parametric: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/summary.ctmm.html
Best,
Chris

Hi Luke,

i. Random intercepts don't really do anything: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2656.13087
Random slopes are worth trying if you can't get anything out of the individual RSFs but want to try to get something out of the population. You can do this to a degree with mean(rsf.fit()), if the individual likelihoods increase on the order of 1 by including the parameter of interest, but a random-slope model is slightly more permissive, and could potentially tease out population-level significance from many individuals with weaker individual-level support (the weaker the support, the more individuals you would need). But not accounting for the autocorrelation is also going to return false positives, so if you don't address that, then you might think you are getting something out but are just getting noise.

ii. I don't see the issue, but maybe I'm not fully understand what you are doing. The distribution of kill/bet sites is what it is. Either the data are representative of that distribution or the sample is biased, and if its the latter, then you would have to adjust for that in some other way in the model.

Definitely do a sensitivity analysis on the parameter estimates by doubling the number of available points until convergence.

1. It depends on how the weights enter into the model - they need to weight the log-likelihood itself. If you can give me a reference, then I can tell you. But, in principle, yes.

2. You need both, because you are using glm as a round-about way of approximating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model. The weights used in rsf.fit() don't need to include that because ctmm is directly evaluating an inhomogeneous Poisson point process model.

3. Not yet, but I'm about to put in support for that.

4. Yes.

Best,
Chris
